# Review of `NeuroStore_Colab_Benchmarks.ipynb` and the reinforced v2 notebook

*Generated by `python colab/make_review.py` from `colab/review_evidence.json` (measurements on v1's own code) and
`colab/validation_cpu.json` (executions of v2). Every number below is a placeholder resolved from those files.*

## Verdict

v1 is an honest, readable scaffold. It runs **unchanged** on JAX 0.12.0.1 (backend: cpu) with no errors, its
disclaimers are accurate, its timing loop (warm-up, `block_until_ready`, device-resident vs transfer-inclusive) is
sound for what it times, and it records hardware metadata. The problems are not crashes; they are about **what the
experiments can show**:

1. Three of its six experiments **cannot fail** (saturated at their operating points), so they cannot support a robustness claim.
2. Nothing carries an interval, and the one comparison that is not saturated (exact vs Hopfield) is **within noise** at
   the sample size used.
3. At its problem sizes an accelerator is **launch-bound**, so the cross-hardware comparison would not separate a CPU from a GPU/TPU.
4. A handful of code-hygiene defects (non-idempotent results list, thin provenance, seed arithmetic, tail percentiles from 8 samples).

v2 keeps the structure and the disclaimers, fixes these, and adds 23 recorded experiment groups, a closed-form
check on the data generator, and self-checks that run on every backend. **v2 has only been executed on a CPU
(JAX 0.12.0.1); nothing was run on a GPU or TPU**, so accelerator-specific behaviour is untested here (see
*What was not validated*).

## How the review was done

* Executed the original notebook unchanged (only `/content` redirected to a scratch directory): no errors.
* Each suspicion became a measurement in `colab/review_experiments.py`, run on the original's own functions
  (28 s on CPU) and stored in `colab/review_evidence.json`.
* v2 was executed through a real Jupyter kernel by `colab/validate_v2.py`; the record is `colab/validation_cpu.json`.
* The v2 sources were linted with pyflakes (clean) and are covered by `tests/test_colab_helpers.py` (NumPy helpers, including a
  Monte-Carlo check of the analytic recall formula) and `tests/test_colab_notebook.py` (static rules; optional end-to-end run).

GPU/TPU dispatch was **not measured here**; host dispatch plus synchronisation on accelerators is commonly reported as tens of microseconds or more (general knowledge, not a result of this review), which would be comparable to or larger than the arithmetic at these sizes, so v1's comparison may show little difference between devices. | Dispatch floor, N sweep to the memory limit, batch sweep, achieved GFLOP/s and GB/s, launch-bound flag. |

**What v1 did well:** explicit scope disclaimers; seeded NumPy generators; steady-state timing with
`block_until_ready`; paired queries across methods; a calibration set separate from the test set for OOD; metadata
capture; the batch-latency vs request-latency distinction in the text.

## What was validated, and how

`colab/validate_v2.py` executes the notebook through a Jupyter kernel and records the result in `colab/validation_cpu.json`.

| Run | Wall time (s) | Cell errors | Result rows | Plots | Self-checks passed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `smoke` (1 CPU device) | 28 | 0 | 286 | 10 | 13/13 |
| `multidev` (smoke profile, 4 virtual CPU devices) | 30 | 0 | 289 | 10 | 14/14 |
| `quick` (1 CPU device) | 270 | 0 | 686 | 10 | 13/13 |

Self-checks (each is an invariant that must hold on **every** backend; a FAIL on a new runtime means that runtime's
numbers need explaining before they are trusted):

| Check | multidev run |
|---|---|
| S1 exact-search recall agrees with the analytic model (\|z\| <= 4.5) | PASS |
| S2 Hopfield(beta=8192) equals exact search wherever the best score is unique (noise 0.3) | PASS |
| S2 Hopfield(beta=8192) equals exact search wherever the best score is unique (noise 0.4) | PASS |
| S2 float32 JAX Hopfield agrees with a float64 NumPy reference (>= 99% identical predictions) | PASS |
| S3 f32/bf16(acc32)/int8/popcount kernels all select a maximal-score pattern | PASS |
| S4 every kernel in the N sweep selects a maximal-score pattern | PASS |
| S5 exact-search recall in the FlyHash comparison matches the analytic model | PASS |
| S5 every WTA code has exactly k active units | PASS |
| S6 VSA decode accuracy matches the closed-form prediction for every (D, k) | PASS |
| S7 scatter/gather SDM is bit-identical to the dense-mask SDM | PASS |
| S8 partial_0.5 is indistinguishable from known-25%-noise (AUROC of max_cos within [0.45, 0.55] and CI contains 0.5) | PASS |
| S9 fault-free exact recall matches the analytic model at the chosen operating point | PASS |
| S10 data-parallel and memory-sharded results attain the maximal score (match the single-device reference) | PASS |
| S11 JAX sparse-accumulate kernels match the NumPy reference | PASS |

Findings printed by the `quick` run on CPU (indicative only; these are CPU numbers and say nothing about accelerators):

- Noisy recall: 33% of the (N, noise) cells have an analytic error probability below 1e-9, so only 67% can separate methods.
- Exact vs Hopfield at N=128, noise 0.4 (exact recall 0.975): paired difference -0.007 [-0.016, +0.003], McNemar p=0.267, 2.0% of queries differ -> no detectable difference.
- Exact vs Hopfield at N=512, noise 0.4 (exact recall 0.922): paired difference -0.010 [-0.024, +0.004], McNemar p=0.2, 4.8% of queries differ -> no detectable difference.
- Exact vs Hopfield at N=2048, noise 0.4 (exact recall 0.862): paired difference -0.052 [-0.073, -0.032], McNemar p=7.24e-07, 13.4% of queries differ -> Hopfield worse.
- Kernels at N=8192, Q=256: speed relative to f32_highest: f32_default 1.00x, bf16_acc32 0.97x, bf16_bf16out 0.84x, packed_popcount 1.43x; popcount memory is 0.031x of f32.
- Scaling: 0% of N-sweep rows are within 5x of the dispatch floor (12 us); best achieved 468 GFLOP/s and 2.0 GB/s at N up to 32768.
- Single-request latency (Q=1, f32): device_resident: p50 5796 us, p99 8906 us; host_roundtrip: p50 6271 us, p99 10789 us.
- FlyHash vs controls at N=512, 30% flips: exact_flat 1.000, fly_gauss_m2048_k64_f16 0.717, fly_m2048_k128_f16 0.930, fly_m2048_k64_f16 (v1) 0.733, fly_m2048_k64_f64 0.711, fly_m8192_k256_f16 0.999, simhash_2048b 1.000, simhash_512b 0.979. v1 FlyHash code: bitmap 256 B, index list 88 B, entropy bound 51 B, against 64 B for the raw input.
- VSA at D=4096: decode accuracy stays >= 0.9 up to k=135 bundled pairs and falls below it at k=187; tuple-level record accuracy 1.000-1.000.
- SDM: best configuration reliably (>=90% exact) stores 200 patterns; its memory per reliable pattern is 184x-369x that of a flat bit-packed store.
- SDM: 47/72 noisy-cue cells return output with more bit errors than the cue.
- OOD chimera family AUROC: max_cos 0.30, margin_top1_top2 1.00, neg_entropy 0.42, logsumexp 0.12 (0.5 = chance).
- Fault injection: first significant degradation of exact search (severity): bitflip 0.01, stuck_zero 0.05, stuck_pos 0.05, dead_rows 0.01, dead_cols 0.05, gauss_static 0.25, lognormal_gain 0.3, read_noise 0.01, adc_bits 6.0.
- Sparse accumulate: N=1024: sparse 4.37 ms vs dense 2.75 ms; N=4096: sparse 7.93 ms vs dense 37.2 ms; N=16384: sparse 13.4 ms vs dense 630 ms; N=65536: sparse 45.4 ms (dense does not fit).

## What was not validated

* **No GPU or TPU was available.** Everything accelerator-specific is untested: the speed of `f32_default`, bf16 and int8 relative to
  `highest`; whether the default precision uses TF32 or bf16 passes and stays exact (the self-check will say); `lax.approx_max_k`
  (guarded by try/except); `Device.memory_stats()` (may return `None`; the notebook then falls back to conservative limits);
  int8 `dot_general` on older TPU generations; compile time of the scan-based popcount kernel; real multi-core scaling.
* **Colab's own Python and JAX versions were not available**: the notebook ran on Python 3.13.18 with JAX 0.12.0.1. A test rejects f-string syntax that needs Python 3.12+, and the code sticks to long-standing JAX APIs (jit, `lax.top_k`, `approx_max_k`, `population_count`, `scan`, `fori_loop`, `jax.sharding`), but no older JAX release was run.
* The profile sizes were chosen from CPU timings (`quick` took 270 s here). On a GPU/TPU the sweeps are bounded by
  `nmax_acc` and a per-sweep wall-clock budget, and any early stop is printed, but the first accelerator run is the real test.
* Timings are machine-specific and relative; a Python-driven loop adds dispatch cost to every measurement (reported as the dispatch floor).
* Fault injection is functional, not a calibrated FeNAND/crossbar/compute-in-memory model; energy, endurance, ADC/DAC power and area are not measured.

## How to use

```bash
python colab/build_notebook.py            # colab/src/*.py -> colab/NeuroStore_Colab_Benchmarks_v2.ipynb
make test                                 # static notebook tests + helper tests (no JAX needed)
make colab-validate COLAB_PY=/path/to/venv/bin/python   # execute smoke + 4-device runs (needs jax, nbclient, ipykernel, pandas, matplotlib)
make colab-review COLAB_PY=/path/to/venv/bin/python     # regenerate review_evidence.json and this file
```

In Colab: upload `colab/NeuroStore_Colab_Benchmarks_v2.ipynb`, pick a runtime, run all cells with `PROFILE = "quick"`, download the
ZIP, repeat on another runtime, then use cell 13b (`COMPARE_GLOB` or `COMPARE_UPLOADS`) to merge runs. Edit the sources in
`colab/src/`, never the generated `.ipynb`; a test fails if they disagree.

## Relationship to the NeuroStore Python prototype in this repository

The notebook's source report (FlyHash / SDM / VSA / Hopfield / FeNAND claims) is a different design from the Python prototype
in `src/neurostore` (k-winner-take-all encoder, assemblies, synapse lattice), and numbers do not transfer between them.
Section 11 is the bridge: it runs the prototype's central read primitive (sparse accumulate over a padded CSR with lazy epoch
decay) on the accelerator and checks it against a NumPy reference.
